reviews.text: Perfect mix of fun mini games, cozy foraging, and deck building adventure. The puppet combat artwork is incredible and it's extremely satisfying creating the perfect meal. The story is super fun and the game itself has high replayability, highly recommend!

The first time i saw this game was about a week ago, and i was excited to see how close the release date was. The moment i got the notification that it was available, i bought it immediately! And wow, i can't recommend it enough, its a solid 10/10 from me. I absolutely love the visuals, the sound design during combat, and honestly, every little action throughout the game feels satisfying. The minigames are genuinely fun and never frustrating. None of them feel overly difficult, and the tutorial explains everything clearly without overwhelming the player. You can pet the chicken-like creatures as much as you want, and they make the cutest sounds! Gardening is simple and relaxing, and taking care of animals to collect their resources is just as easy. The combat art style is absolutely gorgeous, and the protagonist is incredibly adorable^-^ Overall, it's a cozy and charming game filled with lovable creatures. At no point did it feel overly grindy, and the combat never felt unfair or too challenging. It's been a joy to play from start to finish. I experienced no crashes, or lag at any given point!

简单来说这是一部瑕不掩瑜的对福瑞控特攻的一菜多吃的作品。 本来只是因为美术和人设入的，没想到这个游戏会同时包含种植+养殖+钓鱼+烹饪模拟+经典风味传菜+卡牌对战+轻度肉鸽（存疑+恋爱模拟（？all in one买了就是赚了 人设很可爱，主要角色的设计都很有特点，不同阵营的特色风格也很鲜明。 剧情上没太多可说的经典收集同伴拯救世界的路线，不过不知道是有前传还是怎么样，开头的过场动画和初期的一些对话看完也没明白世界观设定，推进得有点突兀。而且简中的台词偶有不太能理解的地方。 流程上本来以为是类似牧场物语之类的连续时间流逝，但是实际上划分的早中晚三个时间段各有各的节奏，除了开店环节之外都可以无负担慢慢做，本质慢节奏。 战斗方面，刚上手的时候确实不太好理解，但是多打几次之后大概就懂了。不过有些用词（比如“墩”）对于卡牌游戏接触不多的人来说难以理解，完全可以用更简单的说法。以及虽然选中的卡牌会上移，但是整体上还是不太好辨认（毕竟卡牌颜色和形状在大部分时候是非常相似甚至可以说完全相同的，个人认为可以加上高亮边框之类的） 最后就是有些过场动画和视觉表现有些过于漫长了，节奏上不是很好。（比如钓鱼时每一条鱼都要单独展示好几秒、每天开店都要看一遍上客动画真的有点折磨）
真的很好玩啊都去玩吧 我该睡了还要上早八

整体节奏非常休闲放松 经营餐厅+少量的农场牧场元素+勇士外出探索打材料。基本就是一些轻松有趣的小游戏组合在一起，备菜/上菜/摆盘/卡牌模式战斗等等，摆盘算是重点，玩法比较像背包管理，把属性不同的菜和材料在大棋盘上自由组合，最终效果会影响勇士外出战斗的属性和卡牌种类，当然还有简易钓鱼（大好评！！！ 战斗方面很简单，卡牌点数比怪物的大就能造成伤害（有combo和增益），前面食材配好的话战斗非常轻松 碎碎念： npc和风景和植物动物都好可爱好治愈！！颜色也很美妙！！！有些名字也很有梗！！ 跟美味鸡进行了长达4秒的亲密治愈摸摸互动动画后，转头去旁边箱子里收了个切下来的美味鸡腿，这对吗？ 您管乳糖不耐肚子胀气叫风味魔法？ 噢，好像确实有风味……？ 不能跳稍微有点难受，空格键被封印了

得益于STEAM只能N/A的评价，但是在30多块打包两个游戏给你，也确实不应该太过苛刻。 先说优点： 1、战斗画风很讨喜，角色路上还自言自语讲故事，剪纸+皮影戏+手绘风格，缝的应该是漫野奇谈； 2、整体游戏节奏以城镇到处捡食材，极轻度的农场经营，极轻度的烹饪，然后做食物，送食物给食客吃了赚钱，然后给主要角色做个大餐，选择食材，组成卡组迎接爬塔战斗，感觉像潜水员戴夫的游戏模式； 3、酸甜苦辣咸5种属性，以属性相克为核心，和野怪反复抽牌比大小，也算是一种制作组的创新，大概是参考了Grounded，但也值得鼓励。 然后说缺点： 1、食材收集非常非常的枯燥乏味，但你又不得不做。浇水、收菜、喂食、钓鱼、然后城镇跑一圈采集，农场经营感觉完全去掉更好。 2、卡片加成远不及单纯数值重要，注意，不是尖塔！不是火车！完全不相关，没有ROUGE元素！没有卡组搭配！非要说搭配，就是每个味道都来点（沙漠多2个咸，沼泽多2个苦这种），尽量选高数值的，尽量小卡组，靠弃牌刷新打。 3、关卡设计不合理，最典型的就是第二关沙漠，存档点前的小怪图标结果来个苦味大怪守门。感情第二关第一次去要不就75%撤退，要不就50%死回去呗。然后个别任务中翻不准，比如煎猪毛，要求每个猪毛焦一次，但任务提示明显有误导。 4、塞尔达的收集音效，有点跳戏。 总的来说，就这个价格，也买不了吃亏买不了上当，试试我觉得是可以的，大不了不喜欢就去吃灰呗。

I have finished Beastro and decided to keep the "Not Recommended" rating. Not because I don't like the game, but because I liked it so much that it disappointed me. Here is my full review: [Playtime] A bit short, with 23 hours to reach 100%. It's kinda sad that I couldn't play this game like a farming life sim. It also has about half the playtime of Slay the Spire. The graphics seem to be targeting long-term playtime, so I didn't expect it to be this short. [Graphics] Too demanding for the genre. With this type of game, I prefer graphics closer to Story of Seasons. The 3D camera and free open-world movement feel overkill for this genre. Unreal Engine 5 also doesn't help with the heavy graphical demands. Dev could halve the model polygons and it would still look great. I played this game on Legion Go 1 and had to reduce the graphics to 50% scaling at 800p on medium settings just to reach 60fps. For comparison, the Legion Go 1 can run Forza Horizon 5 at 120fps on medium settings. Also, you can't fully disable motion blur. That said, I do love the style of the roguelite gameplay. [Final feeling after 100%] Dissatisfaction. Not because I hate this game, but because it feels like a missed opportunity. The devs focused on the wrong things during development. They could have made Beastro a roguelite card game with life-sim elements similar to Story of Seasons or Stardew Valley. Instead, they focused on boring cooking minigames with a lack of ingredients, along with fancy, overkill graphics for a game that doesn't need that much. [Message for dev] (Spoiler) If you are still willing to work on this title, I hope you will add more DLC and continue improving the game. I think reducing the graphics and extending the gameplay would help the game attract more players. The closed ending feels very unnecessary. This is not OneShot, Undertale, or any story-focused indie game. There doesn't need to be a reason to stop going out into the wild, it just doesn't make sense. Anyway, thank you for the game, and sorry that I have to give a "Not Recommended" rating, but it suits the current state of the game. --------------------------- [Origital review] I love this game so far, but sorry, I have to give a thumbs down because of game progression. The practice cooking is unnecessarily hard. The ingredients will be gone every time you fail. This wastes a lot of time and effort for rare ingredients that are very hard to get. It took me 15 minutes to get a single tail just to practice cooking. I also failed all 3 running carrots I could get. And this is just early game with ingredients that are supposed to be "easy." How hard is it going to be in the late game?! The punishment for failing practice cooking is too much! At least I can reload the save file if I fail, but then what is the point of losing the ingredient besides inconvenience and frustration toward players? I will change the review if this will be changed in the future. Because this frustrated me so much for the game I want to play!
白天是动物海湾，开店是胡闹厨房，点餐是你有饼吗，晚上是杀戮尖塔。 ———————— 打完追评： 剧情逻辑清晰、角色行动合理，本来期待像《孤独公会》一样，可惜后期出场的角色没有塑造空间。我怀疑这游戏原剧情里地图很大，但养成系统和收集内容支撑不住这么大，最后砍成这么个草草收尾的样子…… 但是这游戏打折只要35人民币啊朋友！折算下来每小时不到2块钱【不是。

Beastro reminds me of a Roblox tycoon game which has been given a AAA facelift. It is genuinely very shallow and deliberately grindy to the point of causing utter boredom. I rarely ask for refunds of games but in this case I did because there is genuinely nothing to see here as what you'll be doing in the first 20 minutes is the same as you'll be doing 2 hours later. Unlike cozy games such as Stardew Valley where you have meaningful choices on how to use your time each day and various paths of progression to take, Beastro locks you into a very specific route that will never change if you replay the game. Worse still is that progression is painfully slow with you getting perhaps a decorative item or new recipe every half an hour. On the subject of recipes, these all use the same three mini-games over and over again for hours but while these are entertaining, you will spend most of your time wandering around while hand-picking randomly placed resources off of the ground like some gloried street sweeper. Don't waste your money on this as it's trying to be too many different games at once and ultimately fails to be even mediocre at all of them. All style but no substance.

很久之前在b站上看到了简单的宣发，这游戏体验下来还是中规中矩，没什么硬伤，但出彩的部分也不多。平淡中带有一点自己的特色。是一个把种田经营、烹饪小游戏和卡牌构筑结合在一起的小拼盘。 乍一看感觉挺有意思，但是详细来看的话，用不同的食材制作的菜肴，步骤永远都是相同的三个小游戏，缺乏了烹饪过程最重要的体验和成就感。在不同菜肴为卡牌构筑带来不同的属性和牌组方面，设想很好，但卡牌游戏实际上是个属性克制+比大小的结合，玩法深度非常浅，给玩家提供的乐趣简单而有限。 或许这就是这个游戏最大的局限性了，能体会到制作组的想法是将这些元素结合起来制作一款氛围轻松，玩法简单易懂的游戏。但是当玩法浅显到缺乏了体验感的时候，就成为了一款游戏难以忽视的硬伤。 ·主线流程预计20h+ ·美术优秀 ·重复性较高 ·适合放松打发时间玩 ·易感到无聊 ·主角超级可爱

TLDR cuz I'm a chronical yapper, 3/5, if you want a fulfilling complex experience of a cozy game, it feels very undercooked, if you just want a silly game to put some hours and has the money to spare or just to support the devs, get it, on this day every honest creative effort should be rewarded and making a game regardless of how simple it is, is not an easy one. full review time - For my brief 2 hours, I'd say it is has a solid idea and great potential, yet to see how the gameplay loop holds up, so far it is very enjoyable, but i cannot in fairness recommend a game based on what it can be on the future, but to be clear, it is ENJOYABLE, and if you have the money and would care to just have this silly game and how it may evolve, not counting on the fact that i may not change at all on the coming months, it is recommended. I need to note that, as i play it, my opinions on this game may change, so far i only played 2 days but i feel like some insight may help with people with similar tastes. For my opinions, all the systems at first glance mash well together, but are very surface level, the plants grow in a night to day cycle so there isn't caretaking or management (so far at least) there, the animals only need to be fed once (you can pet them though, great work guys!), the cooking aspect, unfortunately, doesn't feel like cooking for the most part, the frying minigame is very cool, no problems here, but the cutting will get old very fast, and the throwing minigame barely even feels like cooking something, unless you have a room specifically to throw your ingredients inside 3 big pots in varying distances. The day cycle is, very, VERY lackluster, there isn't time management, all of this is personal opinion, but there are no stakes or planning on the day cycles, you can do everything you want, and when your resources (basically just the grubs for fishing and giving to the animals) are spent for the day, you continue to the next cycle and that's it, i feel the game would benefit on having a more natural day to night cycle and having more opportunities of what to do besides do your day stuff, that are basically open the restaurant, go get the tea from the baddie and go home, having more opportunities such as not opening the restaurant at all that day would add a slight level of complexity. The town itself is very pretty, all the art on the game is wonderful and the models are really good, but it feels way to big to how small the activities to do are, you walk around and gather resources and there is not really any reason to even wanting to talk to the NPCs on the town, essentially so far on my gameplay, all i have is the crow siblings and the shop guy and the first caretaker, and they don't feel like characters at all, i feel like also adding a separate relationship chart for the townsfolk would benefit the game a little more on it's dept, i like characters and i like to meet them, specially when all of them look so great, please don't be a stationary guy to upgrade things for me and sit there all day with only a single line. That's another aspect that would benefit from a natural cycle, routines, the NPCs being able to wonder the town and close their shops and just talk with you on a bigger level than "what do you need" or in cutscenes would greatly increase my opinions on this game, I also feel that some better transitions between areas would be good for the flow, this is very my own feelings, but i feel like there is always something wrong between the area to area transitions, something is missing there. I'm also a huge liker of fishing minigames, it is too simple, please work more on it, make it harder, MORE COMPLEX, PLEASEPLEASEPLEASEPLEASEPLEEEASE- On the aspects i like, Generally, everything around the art, everything related to the art is top tier, the characters are incredibly pretty and mesh well with what they are meant to represent, the models actually surprised me a lot, specially the clothes, the art style in general is amazing and i feel that a game so pretty such as this one should reach the full of it's potential, that's the main reason I'm doing this review, I'm not one to do many reviews, my opinion, doesn't really matter for anyone, but it's clear that the artists put their hearts on this project, and as much as i can't in fairness recommend this game on this state for a general public, i really hope that in the future there will be a day that I'm able to come here and just BOAST about how much this game has improved and how much i recommend it.

My negative review is based on the fact that this game is tagged as a roguelite, but it's not really. Don't get me wrong, the game isn't bad in what it's trying to do, at least as far as I played it. But I bought it under the assumption that this was going to be roguelite with some deckbuilder elements. The dungeon crawling section, to start with, isn't randomized at all. You'll always hit the same nodes in the same order, and fight the same enemies in the same combination, every single time. There are a few different paths you can take, but those paths never change or deviate in any way, and you'll often be forced to take specific paths to pick up quest items. You're also not trying to complete a full run every time, all you're doing a small segment to get to the next rest point to unlock the next part of the story. Additionally, there's very little skill testing involved. Unlike a roguelite, you can't skim through on clever play and unique deckbuilding. You'll hit stat checks in the middle of a run where the enemy will just throw out more damage than you can handle turn after turn, and you're expected to just eat the loss, level up, and come back the next night. So yeah, this is more like an RPG with some life sim elements than a roguelite. Which is fine if that's what you're looking for, but it wasn't what I thought this game was about. I do hope the devs all the best, however.

Initially I was excited to find a good cooking game, but in the end I am incredibly disappointed. Once you beat the final story quest you're locked out of your save file and need to start from scratch. I don't want to keep replaying the game from zero just to try all the routes for the locations. It feels like the game cuts you off right before the mid-game should start. Unless there's going to be more content that lets you continue playing I wouldn't reccommend getting attached to the save or the characters.

Overall this game was fun and enjoyable, but I beat the entire storyline in 14 hours. After beating the last boss, there is no way to continue playing the story or the game, which to me was very disapointing. I barely unlocked half of all the recipes, even with trying to find every item. I loved the art, the characters, and the world, but i didn't even get to play it on PC due to a download issue. instead, played and beaten on Xbox, which again, was a very fun time. Overall i'm only putting not recommend just due to play length, but aside from that this game was fun to play, so i would say try it out.

This is a beautiful, fun, sweet, cute game that absolutely deserves all of the positive attention that it could get. I will address one issue that left a sour taste in my mouth that it appears others have had as well: The End Game. I don't believe that a game needs to be 80 hours long in order to be good. I don't think that a game needs to have an extensive postgame in order to be justified. And to a certain degree, the Thumbs Down aren't entirely incorrect, that the auto-save function seems to lock you into just fighting the final boss and then 'ending' the game. However, what you CAN do is choose to lose and then you can resume playing the game as normal, exploring the dungeons, trying to find all the recipes, unlock all of the ornaments and outfits and the like. But I can also agree how that would be a bitter pill to swallow that you have to intentionally die in order to keep playing the game that you've been enjoying. If I wanted to get a little bit spicy, I would have liked it if, after the end credits rolled, there was some scene along the lines of [spoilers]"The Remnants are closed, but there's still monsters out there, so we need to keep protecting people"[/spoilers] as an excuse to let us keep playing the game, it would leave people a lot less salty. I can't think of a way to slip the word Umami into this review in any kind of a subtle way, so I'll just say: The game is fun. If you're moderately competent at deck builders and minigames, you'll beat the game in about 12 hours, and if you think that 20 dollars is worth 12 hours of entertainment, then this is definitely worth your money.

I tried to like this game; I really did. Seems like the type of game I like to play. However, right off the bat it left a bit of a sour taste in my mouth because we get pretty much NO into to the main character. Our fox spirit gets rescued by him and there is no 'hey my name is so and so' just pretty much 'your alive help me out'. Who is the chef? He never tells us his name we just kind of know because we are playing as him? The game pretty much assumes you know who you are, you know who and where everything is. You can get around just fine and figure things out but I like a little intro to the characters at least. At least the character I'm playing. Game play is interesting though gets a bit repetitive quickly. Also, it is pretty much impossible to play on keyboard and mouse with some of the cooking mini games so a controller is pretty much required. Some people may like it but it just wasn't for me. I ended up requesting a refund from steam simply because after an hour, I probably won't pick this game up again.

14 hours played. Completed on Day 21 with most side content and upgrades unlocked. Beastro is a fantasy RPG deckbuilder mixed with restaurant management, cooking, gathering, and turn-based combat. It has a charming art style, campy dialogue, and a nostalgic mascot-game energy that feels like something from the early PS3 era. Honestly, that charm is what kept me playing. Unfortunately, I can't recommend it in its current state. The best way I can describe Beastro is through its own theme: imagine going to a restaurant and ordering a full-course meal. Everyone tells you the food is delicious. The presentation is great. You sit down expecting something substantial. Instead, you get a really good sandwich. It tastes great, but when you leave, you still feel hungry. That's Beastro in a nutshell. Almost every system introduces a great idea, then stops before it reaches its full potential. The gathering starts off relaxing but quickly becomes repetitive. Every day and night you're collecting ingredients, feeding animals, fishing, and running the same routes. Automation exists, but arrives so late that much of the game has already become routine. The restaurant side suffers from a similar issue. Cooking is presented through Cooking Mama-style minigames, but they barely evolve throughout the entire game. Regardless of the dish you're preparing, you're largely performing the same actions over and over again. The process feels more like an abstraction of cooking than actual cooking. The strongest mechanic by far is the deckbuilding. Ingredients become cards, flavors interact through a rock-paper-scissors style system, and preparing meals directly affects combat performance. It's a clever idea and initially feels like the game's big selling point. When I completed this initial set up, I thought of it as a clever introduction to how the deck could be built. I didn’t think much of it, only the possibilities that come with it. I believe this is it, this is where the game will truly shine. Later on, you will learn to chop up ingredients to help reduce the size and fit more in at the cost of power. You could cook up ingredients to improve flavor and making it stronger. Maybe they would add seasoning to the placed ingredients where you could alter the bars without filling more space. Boiling ingredients to alter the shape. Later, they could even introduce fusing ingredients together via cooking, adding effects that you could cook further with the right skills and ingredients. Messing up your cooking could add negative effects that can be mitigated in future runs with practice. Maybe even have flavors infused into each card, a mix between the flavors two allowing them to affect more cards. Even better, Caretakers having their own special skills that would activate when they have a set of cards used. Like a ritual sequence. Used for big boss fights and hitting really, really hard. Or a lot. Or a special effect exclusive to your Caretaker. I was excited to see what they were gonna show off. The problem is that the system never grows much beyond its introduction. Combat remains relatively simple throughout the game, relying heavily on flavor matching and number comparisons. While there are synergies and effects to consider, the depth never reaches the level that deckbuilding fans might expect. Eventually, upgrades begin increasing card values enough that many encounters become trivial, reducing the need for strategy altogether. The world itself feels similarly underdeveloped. The setting is interesting, but exploration is limited, NPC interactions are sparse, and most progression happens through static maps with little variety. Ironically, many upgrades eventually provide resources that make portions of the adventure maps feel unnecessary, turning what should be rewarding gameplay into filler. That's what ultimately frustrated me. Beastro isn't a bad game. In fact, it's full of good ideas. The story is entertaining, the characters are likable, and the overall atmosphere is genuinely charming. But almost every mechanic feels like the first draft of something that could have been excellent. For a sale price, it's easy enough to recommend to players looking for a casual experience and a unique premise. At full price, however, I don't think the content or depth is there yet. There's a lot of potential here. That's exactly why this review is so critical. I wanted to love this game. Instead, I walked away feeling like I had been served a very tasty appetizer when I was expecting a full meal.

Beastro is a gorgeous game - one that's clearly lovingly made by a passionate team. I don't write a lot of reviews, but this one especially deserves my praise. Beastro goes a lot deeper than its appealing character designs, gorgeous world design and peaceful, undistracting soundtrack. Who'd have thought that a kitchen simulator could combine so well with strategy? Behind its cutesy façade is a roguelight deckbuilder, which turns out to be surprisingly intricate. You effectively build your deck at the start of the day, directly as a result of what ingredients you choose to give to the Caretaker. Initially, it's easy to put your focus more on the flavour balance in the bottom left, but as the fights get tougher, you need to start paying attention to -what- exact ingredients you're putting into their dish, or you won't get too far. Figuring out how to build an extremely strong deck is very satisfying, supplemented by usables you unlock later into the game - some of which are strikingly more powerful than others. If you can get past the "chore simulator" aspects of the game (farming, routinely running around picking up loose ingredients, fishing etc), the rest of it shines wonderfully. I have nothing bad to say about the audio-visual aspects of the game, but the gameplay is not without several minor negatives, a few of which are tricky to ignore. These are admittedly nit-picky, and based on my own subjective experience of the game, so it's probably only relevant to the developers. I've spoilered the below for both gameplay and story spoilers. [spoiler] - Changing decorations in the restaurant is a little unclear; your cursor should ideally begin on the currently-selected decoration, but it instead seems to begin one whatever it likes. Doesn't help that the item is then "ticked", making it seem like this is the active decoration, when the "tick" only signals which one you're pointing at. If that sounds confusing, it's because it is. Should be so much simpler. [/spoiler] [spoiler] - You unlock the ability to automatically water your plants in your garden (arguably the most tedious, boring task the game has to offer) when you're about 80% of the way through the game, which feels FAR too late. [/spoiler] [spoiler] - Learning new recipes and spending Chef Points is confusing. You're never quite sure where your cursor is. I got lost in this menu every single time I opened it. [/spoiler] [spoiler] - I had a side quest since the beginning of the game to give one of the Caretakers some Marshrooms. Despite my best efforts, I was never sure exactly how to acquire these and give them to him, so this went unresolved for the entire game. [/spoiler] [spoiler] - Pressing the left menu button - the "map" button, in most games - briefly opens Panko's tab, just for a split-second, then suddenly flashes over to the Inventory tab, which is pretty jarring. [/spoiler] [spoiler] - Paying 50 gold to reveal fish in the sea is prohibitively expensive at the beginning of the game, and only feels even SLIGHTLY worth it by the final chapter. This should ideally start cheaper and scale up with each chapter you progress through. [/spoiler] [spoiler] - When offered to upgrade a card by a spirit, pressing (X) to view the description of one of the 5 cards in your hand doesn't do anything. [/spoiler] [spoiler] - Some fights, such as the long-tongue frog boss, have forced segments where you're not able to target or attack the boss themselves. This artificially slows down the fight and removes player agency over their own strategy. [/spoiler] [spoiler] - The final boss, while dramatic, is basically "press discard until you get a purple card". You're effectively punished for bringing in a deck that's too varied. Ideally the final boss should challenge your game knowledge and amalgamate the things you've learned about the deckbuilding mechanic up to now, which should encourage a more varied deck. [/spoiler]

I leave this game a review so that hopefully the devs will see it and follow through with some feedback: i wish i could leave a neutral or mixed review. I think this game has potential, but there would need to be some considerable reworks. The positives: i enjoy the worldbuilding, art direction, basic card system, and methods of storytelling that the game does. The use of color, shapes, and sound all bring together quite a lovely and intriguing world. The way of telling our character how the combat character's days went through a puppet show is such a cool and cute idea story wise, and does put a little distance between you and those characters. The character designs are well done and convey their personalities and backgrounds fairly well. The negatives: the cooking shift minigames every day are downright boring and repetitive until you feed your customers who'll be the ones you do the combat with, in which you do the deckbuilding segment, but i still wish there was more actual cooking to both the deckbuilding and the customer serving it rather than what just feels like a cooking theme, esp if we're supposed to be playing from the perspective of a chef. I feel like it should say smth that the only minigame i actually enjoyed and felt like i was cooking with was the saute one but even then i feel like there could be more to it. More in depth thought: Within my playtime, i have strongly wanted there to be more... effort? thought? put into many of the segments of the gameplay. Currently, I find myself rushing through the day to get to the cardbuilding segment, wishing the cooking was far more engaging and finding that i sometimes build my deck poorly in my haste to get to actually enjoyable gameplay. The game pitches a very strong concept, having stories of our caretakers told tby them to us through the perspective of one who ensures they have the fuel they need to take on their adventures rings a bit hollow when the portion of doing that for them feels so repetitive and boring. It unfortunately comes across almost like the actual cooking part of the game, the main thing our pc does with their day, was an afterthought when it came to implementation and makes you feel less connection with your character's perspective. Im regularly looking for new cooking games that give me a genuine feeling of cooking and thought this could be one of them but it missed the mark and I'm hoping that changes. I've enjoyed my time in the world exploring the concepts theyre putting out there and finding out new things about how it works, but i get to the main gameplay and it feels....hollow, which leads me to less motivation to continue launching it and playing it further at the moment. As another review said, its like showing up to a restaurant that's well liked and praised for its meals, only to walk away hungry having only been served a small appetizer. Unless the systems change for the better, I can't see myself changing my review.

There are a lot of things that are good about this game, but I found that I couldn't recommend it because I ended up just finding it tedious. The recipe and flavour system is actually quite well done in terms of mechanics, however the 'choices' of recipes are an illusion, because in general there is no real choice as you will only generally have one option to choose from that has unlocked by the time you get a new chef point, based on what items the adventurers have picked up while out and about. The concept of being a chef and staying home to farm and gather and create for others is a good one. However you are doing the same things over and over again. There isn't enough variety if you want to get everything; tending your crops, looking after the animals, fishing, gathering out in town etc. You do the same every day and every night, and it fast got boring. The battle system is decent, with you having to create foods specifically for different areas, but you aren't always going to win (which is a good thing, that would be poorly balanced if you did), but if you don't, then you end up back to more tedious gathering, more mini games (some of which I was terrible at), and just ... doing the same thing to prep for the next attempt, which when you are dealing with the bosses, may be several times, and other trips to get more ingredients. Again, having to spend a good amount of time doing the same things was boring, and while eventually you can hire someone to gather in town for you, it really didn't help much since that didn't tackle other daily tasks. Sometimes the story of a game can pull me through games that are flagging in other areas, but I didn't find the story compelling enough. It is a children's story though, so I wasn't using that to base my decision on. But yeah, while the game does have some really interesting mechanics, and it is fun while you are still early on in it, by the time I got 3/4 through the game, I was done with it. The fun was gone, the challenge was just grinding the same thing over and over again. That's why I can't recommend it. I never did complete the game, and I'll be uninstalling it instead. I don't play things I don't find fun.

Very cute game! General gameplay loop is gathering materials and doing chores around town in a light cozy life sim > a minigame-focused little restaurant sim > tableau-builder to make a deck for... > Trick-taking deck-builder adventure to collect more ingredients and advance the story. It sounds a little weird but works surprisingly well [b]for the most part[/b]. The cozy life sim is very cute and sweet, but the novelty wears off and eventually it feels like chores. Admittedly, most of the minigames aren't very engaging - the variety is fun for a little bit, but they still get stale pretty quick. By the end-game, you won't really need money anymore and suddenly the restaurant sim section feels altogether pointless... But that's okay, because the strongest part of the game by far is the back-half of the loop: The deckbuilder adventures! Both planning out your tableu to make the best deck you can and the actual adventure are very fun all throughout. The real star of Beastro is definitely the visual design - the game's art direction is darling! 3D models are fun, lively shapes with super expressive motions. Your team, the creatures, the generic villagers, the shopkeepers, the spirits - [i]Everyone[/i] is a delight! But that's only half of it! Your adventure sections are being "retold" by a a paper-puppet show - and the 2D paper puppet designs are an incredible treat! The puppets themselves and the presentation of those sections had me smiling ear to ear the entire time - it's all extremely cute. To be honest, my biggest complaint is that the game doesn't come with a Gallery feature - I would adore a way to review any paper puppets the player has seen. Overall, very visually beautiful game with a fun main mode and some vestigial minigames. The art design alone is worth the cost of admission. Big recommend to folks who appreciate bright & colorful worlds with unique and different lore (especially furries). Also recommend to folks who like cozy games, but wish they had a little bit extra to them.

[h3] Great Concept But Combat is to Rock Paper Scissors [/h3] The concept of the game is unique, I just find the choirs during the day and night time to be a little to tedious. The card roguelite combat is interesting but is very rock paper scissors heavy meaning you can get unlucky match ups. [b] Gameplay Loop [/b] The day is split to 3 sections, morning, evening and night. Morning is where you check your farm, feed your animals collect their by product, run around town collecting other ingredients scattered around town, fish and visit vendors. I personally found this part too boring for my taste, it was fun at first but got to repetitive, maybe they should have limited everything to the farm instead of having you run everywhere around town. Afternoon is where you run your actual restaurant, this part consist of 2 parts, one where you feed customers that give you money and second where you feed your hero to make their deck. The afternoon section I have no problems with and was the most fun part of the game. Night is where you can run around town collecting ingredients that show up at night only, fish (there are different fish at night). And where you actually do the roguelite portions of the game. [b] Combat [/b] This is where most of my complaint is. Conceptually it has potential but you can get punished hard not because you played bad but simple because you had a bad matchup. In most turn base games that have this rock paper scissors mechanic, you general take more damage on your elements your weak to, deal bonus to elements your strong against and deal neutral damage if your not weak or strong against an element. In this game there is weakness, strength but no neutral. There are 6 "elements"(the six element you don't have access to right away), each element is weak to another element and can strengthen another element. For example, green element is weak to blue and can strengthen purple. So if an enemy plays a green card, I can only do 2 things play a blue card, this weakens green card's atk by half or I can play green and add a purple ontop of it to make my green card do 1.5x more damage. Damage is determined by who has the higher atk if I have 5 atk and enemy has 2, the enemy takes 5 damage and I take 0. Any other element besides green or blue will have no effect and you will take full damage. Meaning if I don't want to take full damage at any turn only 2/6 of the elements are useful, the rest do nothing and that's assuming the cards you have for those 2 elements have mare attack then the enemy or you will still take full damage. Also it cost hp to top up your hand with max cards (5) and even more hp to discard your hand and draw a new one. General deck size ranging from 10 to 15 and with 6 elements your stretched pretty thin on the amount elements you can have. Realistically your first time fighting bosses and enemies you have no idea what cards they have so you build a balance deck with all elements and you will be fighting enemies that have decks specialized in 2 or 3 elements and your all rounder deck is going to get rekted. It's only upon the second attempt do you have knowledge and can craft a better deck to fight the enemy. When making your deck the game does incentive you to diverse your deck because if your deck hits certain thresholds for each element you get bonus hp. [b]Conclusion[/b] I think the game is unique but the daily choirs gets to repetitive and the combat can feel one sided at times, where you lost simple from making the safest choice when confronted with no knowledge of the enemy you are fighting in a rock paper scissors system.

The cooking elements of the game, which I expected to be a focus, ended up being repetitive, boring, and downright luck-based and frustrating at some of the higher levels. Additionally, about half of my play time was taken up by just daily, mundane gathering of ingredients. Crops and animals, barely need to be attended to beyond basic feeding and fetching of the necessary feed, while the search for randomly spawned ingredients involved running around the whole map for 10 minutes, scrutinizing the ground and walls while. Additionally, the story is incredibly short. I honestly expected the game to have a few more regions and more characters to play with, given the direction things were going. Likewise, the writing didn't feel that strong, and a lot of major conflicts were resolved with a pat on the back and a kick in the pants. To make matters worse, the game offers absolutely no replayability once the end is reached. Your save literally cannot progress beyond the final fight, unless you either purposefully lose or don't engage with it at all. The game *does* warn about this, albeit vaguely. Finally, there are numerous areas of the game that lack polish, particularly with continuity errors. For example, a character will exit town as part of the main storyline, but then still be present and will act as though nothing is going on. Also, I had characters move in to town without actually fulfilling the requirements for them to do so. I have no idea how this happened. I think that Beastro had a lot of potential and still does, and I'd really like to see more from it, given that I'd looked forward to it for a while. Like I mentioned, the lore that you are tantalizingly drip-fed is genuinely fascinating and carried a lot of my enjoyment of the game. Plus, all the food and characters are just fun to look at and think about. So cool! Ultimately, it is a fun, yet short experience that is a little rough around the edges. I really wish I could leave a neutral review... I just think a couple touch-ups could go a long way.

While I do recommend checking out this game, it is not one I'd pay full price for. As it is, this game is a dish that was pulled out of the oven mid-cooking and served while still raw inside, with slap-dash garnish added last minute to make it feel like it kinda has a purpose. I'm only saying "recommended", because the parts that are good are good enough to sorta kinda make it worthwile to try it out. I was so tremendously excited for this game to release, because I absolutely adored the demo. I love cooking sims, I crave farming sims that aren't totally automation-focused, building up a village is always a treat, and the conceit of feeding the fighters to build their decks for when they go out sounded like it could have some real depth. Unfortunately, after the first few hours the game largely runs out of steam. The farming is fine, but you have to run around the entire town every single day to gather ingredients. This could've been okay if there were more things to do around town, but none of the NPCs have anything new to say, there's nothing to discover, nothing changes in the day-to-day, so it's just empty running. This could have been fixed by having more dialogue, a gift system, or random vignettes, but there's nothing. It would also be nice if the farming had some complexity to it, but it's mostly just pressing the harvest button. The cooking is neat, and there's a nice diversity of dishes and recipes with imaginative ingredients and great art. However, the ingredient learning system is oddly punishing, the minigames get no explanation, and growing the restaurant's popularity/appeal doesn't feel rewarding outside of just getting money. Plus, the differences in ingredient availability are quite extreme, especially considering how you're given no other incentive to go to old areas and, thus, will likely end up with those ingredients being on a timer (unless you want to just halt progress for a few days, which again means more tedious running around). Making dishes for the fighters (caretakers) is great fun at first, implying a lovely balancing act between fulfilling their desires and anticipating what you'll need without making too bloated of a deck, but the game punishes cleverness. Bosses are orders of magnitude more difficult than any of the other content, so essentially you need to build a deck that has the bare minimum of cards to counter an area's primary flavor, then try to stack your deck to specifically counter the boss, because you really can't do both. The rock-paper-scissors nature of things means a card is either useful or it isn't, and if you don't have useful cards, mulligan until you do. So, rather than feeling like you're piecing together an intricate strategy, you're just trying to get as many big numbers of the right type as you can, cheapening the whole fantasy. It's still a beautiful game, with wonderful designs and excellent use of color and some really nice music, but it would need some fundamental changes to really meet its potential.

This is a really interesting game to me. I come as someone that enjoys doing seemingly mundane tasks, like preparing meals in Vintage story, and I also like roguelikes and deckbuilders. But right now, the cooking part (which I expect to be center to gameplay, and not a side activity to the true point of the game, combat) is mind numbing after only a few days, because you do not actually cook anything. At the start of each day, you may choose up to 4 meals, but these have no impact on how you will actually cook them. It seems to me that the game choose 3 minigames at random, these minigames are not impacted by the ingredients you pick, at most you will get a cosmetic effect. Once you have finished with the 3 minigames tada! you just poof the meals into existence, on your table, then go serve your customers. I expected the cooking to be much much more complex than that, where you would be able to prepare each ingredient individually, then dress them on their plates afterwards, not just play 3 minigames. The most interesting part of cooking which I actually enjoyed, is preparing meals for the caretakes (which are basically your heroes that will venture out of the village and go do quests by slaying monsters, getting their loots, and finding resources to bring back to you). To prepare a meal, you will have to place ingredients on a 5×5 grid. Each of these ingredients has one of six elements ( bitter, sour, salty, umami, sweet, and [spoiler] Spicy [/spoiler]. Elements are important, because in order for your caretaker to have the maximum HP possible, you must fulfill all of his preferences in taste, meaning placing the correct amount of each ingredients. Ingredient placement are important, because tastes interact with each other when ingredients are placed adjacent to each other, for example, umami and bitter will cancel each other, but umami and sour will make each other more potent. Ingredients are doubly important, because when placed, they give you a card (basically an action) that you will use in the fight section later. You must absolutely adapt your deck to the enemies you intend to face, else you will be defenseless. Once you are done with picking your ingredients, you just press F, then go through a cutscene et voilà! Off your caretaker goes (I would have preferred to have some actual cooking gameplay, where my performance would affect how potent each ingredient would be combat wise. Onto the fight now: Each caretaker has it's own deck corresponding to it's flavor (the first one is umami for example) plus one card for each of the ingredients present on the crafting grid of the meal he or she ate. Each round is played like a trick taking game: monsters draw a card at random from their deck, and in order to inflict damage to them, you must play a card of the same color with a higher value, OR play a card with the flavor type that weakens the card played by the monster. For example: you encounter a monster that played a sweet card with an attack value of four. To deal damage to it, you must play a sweet card of a value of 5 ( in which case you will do your card's value - the monster defense card value + your basic attack bonus). OR, you could play a salt card, which will cut the monster's card value by half, which is extremely powerful. You can also empower your attack by using a complementary flavor to your played card to add it's value and effect if any. If you do not play a card of the correct color, the card you played will be ignored, and the monster will inflict full damage to you. Drawing cards in this game is not automatic or done once each turn, instead you can choose to manually refresh your hand, sacrificing a bit of health. You can either refill your hand, which costs 1 hp, or discard everything and draw everything, which costs 2. If you don't have a card to face the monster, you basically have to redraw until you have something, because the costs for discarding are way lower than those you would take by tanking an attack, and it's possible effect. So if you encounter an enemy that plays a card that you didn't foresee, and didn't put a lot of the countering / matching flavor they will mess you up a lot. Appearance wise, this game is gorgeous. Everything is very beautiful, from the 2d cutouts in the fight "recollections", the meals you serve your patrons, and the characters. The only thing I would say is that the animation seem a tad stiff at times. Overall, I am a bit disappointed, because I expected the cooking portion of the game to be much more in depth, but what is there is fairly enjoyable for the price I paid. I am not sure if others will find the price worth it however

If I could leave a "meh" review rather than thumbs up/down I would, but since I have to choose I'm going to say thumbs down for now. I'm parroting someone else a bit when I say this, but Beastro feels like a good, warm, home-cooked meal that means well and should taste great, but someone removed it from the oven too soon and parts of it just didn't get thoroughly cooked. The combat of the game is focused around the different flavors and you get to use "caretakers" who represent each flavor...except you don't. Two are introduced as Non combative merchant NPCs, and their quality of life features appear too late in the game to even make proper use of. The sour caretaker has an assassin theme with throwing knives and poison, but he doesn't participate in fighting at all. This seems like they ran out of production time or money and had to scrap portions of the game. Some other quality of life features, such as for your garden, also dont appear until the very end of the game, making them only briefly useful. The cooking mini games are odd. The boiling game was very difficult to get a "fantastic" score but you can spam the button in the chopping board game and miss several times and still get a "fantastic" rating. Also what is with the animal characters not having tails? You can call it an artistic choice, but it seems like another cut content that should have been there. I actually have nothing bad to say about the combat other than missing out on the non combative caretakers. I really liked making the meals and min/maxing my card builds. If they have a major content update in the future that fixes these issues I've seen many people discuss then I'll leave a better review because it is a good game, it just needs some seasoning and a little more time in the oven.

[h3] Things I like: [/h3] - There is a lot of variety in the gameplay due to the employment of multiple archetypes; ranging from resource gathering & restaurant management, to Mario-Party-style minigames & a full-on RPG combat system. - The combat system & flavor system are amazing. The hexagonal relationship among flavors has been well thought-out and is a creative way to blend the story with the core gameplay. The card-based combat loosely reminds me of Magic: The Gathering, but still feels unique and provides an addicting challenge. - The tutorials go into complete detail to explain how the game works, leaving little room for ambiguity whilst also not sounding too bloated. That's how tutorials should be! - Just as with the combat system, the story is unique and its worldbuilding has been well thought out. I like the idea of a world where denizens are based around flavors and the magic system is likewise. - The characters are cute, funny, and full of personality. Even the livestock NPCs (e.g., delishkens, fenpires) make the game feel alive. - The art style is great. Clearly some furries were in charge of this--only [b]they[/b] know how to make anthropomorphic creatures look this good. ;3 The way color is used is also good. - The music is great and fits the environment & atmosphere. The same can be said of the sound engineering, which fit the actions & creatures they're assigned to. - The game's price is appropriate. - The dev team has been quick to fix bugs. Many of said bugs have been minor, which is a rare sight to see from an indie studio. [h3] Things I don't like: [/h3] - The game is too short. [b][u]I'd happily pay for a story expansion![/u][/b] - There are too few regions to explore and the maps do not have enough variety/randomness to them. Earlier maps, like the Marshlands, eventually feel too easy & predictable to justify returning to. Maybe consider implementing a procedural generation system? - There are too few venture caretakers to choose from; [spoiler]only three to be exact: Oyshi (Umami), Azur (Sweet), and Kalan (Bitter). There was a missed opportunity to have six caretakers from each of the six flavor realms, but Colsi (Sour) and Sunna (Salty) do not get to be venture caretakers, and Pokosh (Spicy) straight-up becomes an antagonist. [b][i]Frankly, it looks a lot like the devs were (or are) planning to have Sunna, Colsi, and Pokosh be venture caretakers, but had their roles demoted due to time constraints. I hope they reconsider and give them fighting roles for the player to control in an expanded story. [/i][/b][/spoiler] - Because of the above bullet point, some characters don't get as much character development as they deserve. [spoiler]Sunna, for example, has such an uninteresting personality and so little involvement both story-wise & gameplay-wise that I forgot his name when writing this review, and struggled to look it up because apparently other players don't remember his name either--I don't even remember his sex, so I'm assuming male. Colsi feels a little bit more involved because his blunt and "I'm gonna go take a nap" personality is more memorable & unexpectedly hilarious.[/spoiler] - Personally, I do not find flavor crystals useful because adding flavor without adding a card naturally reduces the amount of cards one has access to. I can see how some strategies might rely on a small hand, but for me, more cards = more options. - At the time of writing, the most major bug I've experienced is an ongoing visual bug where characters instantly switch to their next animation with no transition, sometimes causing jiggle/spring bones to bounce all over the place and clip with other parts--a phenomenon most often observed with Kalan's hat and Azur's skirt. It makes animations feel jerky & unfinished. - The game uses Unreal Engine. We need more devs courageous enough to make their own engines instead of relying on other people's broken ♥♥♥♥. - There is a missed opportunity to have custom colors for cosmetic items. - There is a GIANT missed opportunity for additional voice acting. Only the intro features voice acting whereas the rest of the game is purely written dialogue. Why not do what Gears for Breakfast did with [b]A Hat & Time[/b]: have actors voice all of the written dialogue? That would be awesome! Heck, the guy voicing Panko in the Beastro trailers would be a great fit to bring back for the whole game! - There is no multiplayer. I can imagine ways a peer-to-peer PVP mode could be made. [h3]Overall:[/h3] This game deserves praise for its innovative gameplay, original story, and lack of major bugs. There's definitely room to expand the story & gameplay, and I hope the devs capitalize on it with future updates.

I liked this game. The art style and worldbuilding is interesting, and the turn based gameplay is fun (I mean it's a deckbuilder, they're addicting!) The problem is that's...the only highlight of this game. The rest of the game is all cozy game stuff, in the form of everyday chores, and item collection. But unlike titles like Stardew or Animal Crossing, it lacks a fundamental aspect of both of these games: charming NPCs. Every piece of dialogue outside the main story is the blandest of bland one-liners, even from the main characters. This makes the setting feel less like a town and more of an RPG hub, where NPCs are just there to give you services rather than have any actual substance to their characters. Which does Not work for a game where you spend the majority of your time *in town*, collecting items from around the map. It ends up making the non-battle sections feel like unnecessary bloat, when all you're doing in these sections is, essentially, grinding for the actual fun part of the game. It's like if you took Slay the Spire, and put in a bunch of unskippable minigames and a cutscene before every run. And there aren't any charming character interactions to distract you from that! No real goal to work towards other than better cards. If you're going to make it grindy, at least put it in the actual fun part of the game. Which, granted, they do do. But it needs some kind of story in-between if you want something more interesting than just that. On top of that, a lot of major characters had a lot of missed potential as well. Their quests were done too quick, and they lost plot relevance too soon, which -- as previously discussed -- basically stripped away everything interesting about them and relegated them to single lines of dialogue with less substance than a literal vacuum. So yeah. This, among other things, is why I can at best say this game is unpolished, and at worst unfinished. (There's also some choppy animations and sloppy camera work in some places, but those are just nitpicks honestly. Still affects the game's polish though.) They've got the cast of loveable characters. Use them, or the rest of the game suffers for it. Hopefully the devs update the game to address some of these issues moving forward.
